stages.name: Market structures: barriers and monopoly
stages.title: Market structures: barriers and monopoly
stages.sub: Explain why some markets stay closed to new firms, and derive the monopoly profit-maximising equilibrium.

steps.q: A new firm wants to sell electricity but needs a government licence it cannot get. What is stopping it entering?
steps.right: A rule set by government or regulators
steps.wrong: The cost of building power stations
steps.hint: Think about who controls the licence, not the cost of equipment.
steps.pre: That kind of barrier, created by law or regulation, is a

steps.q: A water pipe network only makes sense if one firm builds it, since laying a second set of pipes down every street would be wasteful. What is stopping a rival entering?
steps.right: The way the industry itself is structured
steps.wrong: A rule set by government or regulators
steps.hint: No law bans a rival here. What about the industry makes duplication pointless?
steps.pre: That kind of barrier, arising from the industry itself, is a

steps.q: An existing airline drops its prices to a loss-making level whenever a new airline tries to enter its routes, then raises them again once the new airline leaves. What is stopping entry now?
steps.right: Deliberate action by the existing firm
steps.wrong: A rule set by government or regulators
steps.hint: Is this happening because of a law, or because of what the existing firm chooses to do?
steps.pre: That kind of barrier, created on purpose by firms already in the market, is a

steps.q: Licences, one-firm-only industries and price wars all make it hard for a new firm to get in or get out safely. What do all three count as, together?
steps.right: Different obstacles facing entry and exit
steps.hint: Each one is a different obstacle facing a firm trying to enter or leave a market.

steps.q: A firm spends £2 million building a custom factory that cannot be resold or used for anything else. If it later leaves the market, can it get that £2 million back?
steps.right: No, it is lost for good
steps.wrong: Yes, it can sell the factory on
steps.hint: The factory has no other use and no buyer. What happens to money spent on it?

steps.q: If leaving a market means losing millions that can never be recovered, how easily will firms risk entering it in the first place?
steps.wrong: Just as easily, entry stays equally attractive
steps.hint: Think about the risk of entering if you might not get your money back on exit.

steps.q: An oligopoly has just a few large firms, each spending heavily on branding, factories and legal protections. Could a small new firm easily match this and break in?
steps.right: No, it would find entry very hard
steps.wrong: Yes, entry would be fairly easy
steps.hint: Think about the scale of spending and legal protection already in place.

steps.q: One firm supplies all of a country's rail track, protected by law and owning resources no rival can copy. Could another firm realistically start competing and undercut its price?
steps.right: No, it can set the price largely alone
steps.wrong: Yes, competition would force its price down
steps.hint: With no close rival able to enter, who decides the price in this market?

steps.q: This monopoly firm picks its profit-maximising output using the usual MC=MR rule. Once it has that output, how does it find the price to charge for each unit?
steps.right: Reads the price straight up from its demand curve at that output
steps.wrong: Sets price equal to marginal cost at that output
steps.hint: The firm is a price maker: which curve tells it what buyers will pay for that quantity?
